slides.title: Pleural fluid analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Pleural fluid (thoracentesis); blood is tested at the same time

What it is used for: The analysis looks for the cause of fluid buildup in the pleural space (pleural effusion). Symptoms include unexplained chest pain, dry cough, trouble breathing and fatigue; sometimes the effusion is found by chance on imaging done for another reason. Removing fluid from a large effusion also relieves shortness of breath.

slides.title: Pleural fluid analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: The pleura is a thin tissue covering the lungs and lining the chest wall. A small amount of fluid between its two layers lets them glide as you breathe. According to MedlinePlus, the pleural space normally holds less than 20 mL of clear, yellowish (serous) fluid; an excess is called a pleural effusion.

The laboratory checks the fluid for cancer cells and other cells (for example blood cells), for glucose, protein and other chemicals (including LDH), and for bacteria, fungi, mycobacteria and viruses; culture and cytology are also done.

slides.title: Pleural fluid analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Interpreting the result · 1/3
bullets: The results show which type of fluid is present. Light's criteria are usually used: the amounts of certain proteins (protein, LDH) in pleural fluid are compared with blood to classify the fluid as transudate or exudate.

slides.title: Pleural fluid analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Interpreting the result · 2/3
bullets: Transudate is a watery, low-protein fluid that leaks from blood vessels because of pressure; it is most often due to heart failure, kidney disease or liver disease including cirrhosis. Exudate is a cloudy, high-protein fluid seen with inflammation, infections (pneumonia, tuberculosis), pancreatitis, autoimmune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, lupus), cancer (leukemia, lymphoma, breast or lung cancer) and chest injuries. Exudate from infection may contain pus, bacteria or fungus; from cancer, cancer cells; from injury, blood.

slides.title: Pleural fluid analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Interpreting the result · 3/3
bullets: If infection is suspected, the fluid is cultured. The test is also done when hemothorax (blood in the pleura) is suspected. Causes of effusion also include very low blood protein (albumin) and severe malnutrition.

slides.title: Pleural fluid analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: Fluid is removed by thoracentesis: the patient sits upright with arms resting on a table (or lies on one side), the skin is cleaned and numbed, and a needle is passed between the ribs into the pleural space, often guided by ultrasound. Do not cough, breathe deeply or move during the procedure. Tell the provider about blood thinners; imaging (ultrasound, CT or x-ray) is done before and after.

slides.title: Pleural fluid analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: A pleural fluid analysis alone may not find the specific condition; the results help the provider choose further tests (blood and urine tests, imaging, bronchoscopy, biopsy). MedlinePlus does not give the numeric cut-offs of Light's criteria — they come from laboratory and clinical guidelines, so they are not listed on this card.

slides.title: Synovial fluid analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Joint fluid (arthrocentesis, sterile syringe)

What it is used for: The analysis helps find the cause of joint pain and inflammation: osteoarthritis, gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition (pseudogout), rheumatoid arthritis, joint effusion, joint infection, or a bleeding disorder such as hemophilia. Symptoms include joint pain with fever, swelling, redness, warmth and difficulty bending the joint. It may also be used to monitor a known joint condition.

slides.title: Synovial fluid analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Synovial fluid cushions the ends of bones and reduces friction during movement; normally there is only a small amount. It is usually light yellow, clear and a little sticky or stringy. In joint disease, extra fluid builds up and causes pain, stiffness and inflammation.

The laboratory checks the colour and clarity of the fluid; counts red and white blood cells and looks for crystals (in gout) or bacteria under the microscope; measures glucose, protein, uric acid and LDH; and cultures the fluid for bacteria.

slides.title: Synovial fluid analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Interpreting the result
bullets: Abnormal fluid may be cloudy, or thicker or thinner than normal. Blood suggests a joint injury or a bleeding problem; pus, a joint infection; too much fluid, osteoarthritis or cartilage, ligament or meniscus injury; evidence of gout or pseudogout (crystals), inflammatory conditions treatable with medicines.

slides.title: Synovial fluid analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: Fluid is taken by arthrocentesis (joint aspiration): the skin is cleaned and numbed, a sterile needle is inserted into the joint space and fluid is drawn into a sterile syringe; it usually takes 1–2 minutes. Fasting for several hours is sometimes required. Tell the provider about blood thinners such as aspirin, warfarin or clopidogrel — they can affect the results or the procedure.
Limitations: Specific results depend on what abnormalities were found. To understand them, the provider considers your symptoms, medical history and other test results.

slides.title: Effusion fluids: transudate and exudate
bullets: Effusion fluids that collect in serous cavities consist of blood plasma, lymph and tissue fluid; serous membranes have parietal and visceral layers, and mesothelial cells of the inner layer make the serous fluid.
Lymphatic vessels communicate with serous cavities through special openings, so even a slight blockage of drainage can lead to fluid collecting in the cavity.
A transudate is fluid that collects in serous cavities without inflammation (in the pericardium, abdomen and pleural cavity); it is usually clear, colourless or pale yellow.

slides.title: Effusion fluids: transudate and exudate
bullets: Causes of transudate: venous congestion (circulatory disturbance, kidney disease, cirrhosis), raised capillary permeability, lowered oncotic pressure of the blood (less protein and albumin), blocked lymph vessels, electrolyte disturbances and increased aldosterone production.

An exudate is fluid that collects in body cavities as a result of inflammation; microflora and viruses, parasites, bile, pancreatic or intestinal fluid entering the cavity, and spread of tumour cells into the serous cavity all matter in its formation.

slides.title: Types of exudate (by macroscopic appearance)
bullets: Serous exudate — clear or turbid, yellowish or colourless (depends on the bilirubin content).
Serous-purulent and purulent — turbid, yellow-green, with abundant sediment; in pleural empyema, peritonitis and others.
Putrid — sharply foul-smelling, turbid, grey-green; typical of lung gangrene and processes with tissue breakdown.

Haemorrhagic — red or brown; in tumours, injuries, pulmonary infarction, pleurisy and haemorrhagic diatheses; when a malignant tumour spreads along the serous membrane the exudate may also be clear and serous.

slides.title: Types of exudate (by macroscopic appearance)
bullets: Chylous — milky and turbid (fat droplets), clears on adding ether; chyle-like — milky because of fatty degeneration of cells, stays turbid or clears slightly with ether (liver cirrhosis, malignant tumours).
Cholesterol (typical of long-standing exudates), mucous, fibrinous and mixed (serous-haemorrhagic, mucous-haemorrhagic, serous-fibrinous) exudates are also distinguished.

slides.title: Telling a transudate from an exudate
bullets: Rivalta test: when the fluid is dropped into a narrow cylinder with a weak acetic-acid solution, a drop of transudate dissolves before reaching the bottom; if the drop leaves a turbid trail behind, the fluid is an exudate.
Relative density: 1.006–1.015 in a transudate, above 1.018 in an exudate.
Protein: below 30 g/L in a transudate, above 30 g/L in an exudate; a transudate does not clot, an exudate does.

slides.title: Telling a transudate from an exudate
bullets: LDH ratio (fluid/serum): below 0.6 in a transudate, above 0.6 in an exudate; cell count (nucleated cells): below or above 1×10⁹/L; cholesterol: below or above 1.6 mmol/L.
In an exudate microbiological examination may find microflora (streptococci, staphylococci, pneumococci, E. coli and others); a transudate contains no bacteria.

slides.title: Telling a transudate from an exudate
bullets: Sediment cytology: a transudate has mesothelium, lymphocytes, sometimes erythrocytes; an exudate has neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, erythrocytes, eosinophils, reactive mesothelium or tumour cells.

slides.title: Sampling and microscopy of exudate
bullets: Fluid is collected into two containers: an EDTA tube (so the puncture fluid does not clot; cell count is done in the Goryaev chamber or on a haematology analyser) and a clean dry tube (for biochemistry — protein, glucose and others).

After the cell count, the fluid is centrifuged to obtain sediment; at least 2 smears are made from each layer, air-dried and stained by standard methods (Romanowsky–Giemsa, Pappenheim–Kryukov, Leishman and others).

By cell content the exudate may be reactive (mainly mesothelial cells), reactive-inflammatory (with neutrophils), strongly lymphoid, eosinophilic (eosinophils above 10%), macrophagic, or containing cancer cells.

slides.title: Sampling and microscopy of exudate
bullets: Eosinophilic exudate is found in immune-complex reactions on contact with allergens, parasites, drugs and tumours.
Under unfavourable influences mesothelial cells change, and telling them from tumour cells becomes difficult.
Malignant tumours of serous membranes are primary (mesothelioma) or secondary (metastatic).

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: fluid/serum protein >0.5 or LDH ratio >0.6 or fluid LDH > 2/3 of serum ULN ratio

slides.title: Pleural fluid is cloudy and high in protein. Which type is it by Light's criteria, and which cause fits better?
options: Exudate — e.g. pneumonia, tuberculosis or cancer
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. Cloudy, high-protein fluid is typical of exudate.

Basis: Exudate: high protein, from inflammation, infection or cancer; transudate: watery, from heart, liver or kidney disease.

slides.title: What is the Rivalta test intended for:
options: Determination of hemoglobin in serous fluid
Determination of cells in serous fluid

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of examining transudates and exudates?
bullets: 1. Analysis of body cavity fluids (pleural, ascitic, pericardial) determines the mechanism of fluid accumulation (transudate or exudate) and the cause.
2. Transudate – disturbed hydrostatic/oncotic pressure (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome): protein and LDH low, few cells.

3. Exudate – inflammation or tumor (pneumonia/empyema, tuberculosis, tumor, pancreatitis, autoimmune): one of Light's criteria – fluid/serum protein ratio >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6 or fluid LDH > 2/3 of serum ULN.

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of examining transudates and exudates?
bullets: 4. Additional tests: cell count and differential, glucose, pH (empyema), amylase, TG (chylothorax), Gram/culture, tests for tuberculosis, cytology (tumor cells); in ascites SAAG.
5. In heart failure on diuretics, Light's criteria may show a transudate as an exudate – the albumin/protein gradient or NT-proBNP helps.

slides.title: Differential diagnosis of transudates and exudates?
bullets: 1. Distinguishing transudate from exudate – Light's criteria: fluid/serum protein >0.5; fluid/serum LDH >0.6; fluid LDH > 2/3 of serum LDH ULN – if at least one is met, it is an exudate.
2. Transudate: clear, pale yellow, low protein, few cells; causes – heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia.
3. Exudate: turbid, cellular, high protein and LDH; causes – infection (parapneumonic, empyema, tuberculosis), tumors, pancreatitis, autoimmune diseases, pulmonary embolism.

slides.title: Differential diagnosis of transudates and exudates?
bullets: 4. Light's criteria wrongly classify 15–30% of transudates as exudates (up to a third in heart failure or cirrhosis on diuretics) – in that case the serum–fluid albumin/protein gradient is more specific; NT-proBNP and additional criteria (cholesterol) are also used.
5. In ascites the serum–ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) is used; the cause of an exudate is determined by the cell differential, glucose, pH, amylase, culture and cytology.
